reviews.content:
Professor Chilton's lectures are extremely engaging.
This class is easy (speaking from someone who doesn't have prior web dev experience). There are only assignments and projects, no exams. Assignments 1-6 helps you practice the web dev stuff you learn in class (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Bootstrap, JQuery, Flask). The Midterm project, which is an individual project, builds on to Assignment 6 (a database website with the topic of your choice) by adding more features and also focusing on graphic design. The Final project, which is encouraged to be done in groups (you choose your own groups as long as your group members are in your TA session, and you can make an exception with your TA to work on it individually), allows you to create a website teaching users a topic of your choice. 
Professor Chilton highly encourages students to use ChatGPT in their assignments and projects, which made this class easy. However, I would encourage you to still engage with the learning process to really benefit from this class. Even if ChatGPT doesn't help, there are 32 TAs holding OHs every week. Note that Professor Chilton does not give out any A+s.
Unlike HWs 1-6 and the projects, some parts in HWs 7-12, which were used to guide students in their final projects, felt like busy work, but I found many parts of them to be very helpful because you can create your prototype and your TA will give you feedback on it. Also, HW instructions often had typos, and I feel like sometimes in the lectures after Spring Break, Professor Chilton repeats the same topics.
Some HWs focused on website functionality, while others focused on both website functionality and graphic design. 
If you want to explore web dev (both the coding and graphic design aspects of it), check out this class!
reviews.workload:
12 (almost) weekly assignments (each counted for 5% of final grade), a Midterm project (10% of final grade), Final project (20% of final grade), participation and attendance in TA sessions after Spring Break (10% of final grade). Lecture attendance is not required, and Professor Chilton posts lecture recordings.
If you follow all the instructions in the HWs and projects and asked for feedback on your work, you will get a 100%. No A+ grades are given out.
BTW: TA sessions are basically these meetings you have with ~10 students and your TA (chosen by you if there's room in the session) each Wednesday after Spring break. Each group talks about their progress on their project/their work in HWs 7-12 and gets feedback from the TA. Before Spring break, lectures were on Mondays and Wednesdays. After Spring break, lectures were only on Mondays, with TA sessions (only 45 mins) being on Wednesdays.

If you're hoping to learn SQL and how to use databases, this class does that... but only for the first few weeks. After that, it is all database management systems, but after the class you do have a pretty good idea of how databases are implemented which is useless for most people at the face level, but very useful for actually using databases. 

Still, the material is boring. Ross lectures as if he understands this fact and has surrendered to his powerlessness in changing it. Every lecture consists of a new topic which he explains well and a few examples. The review lectures are pretty useful. 

Basically, the structure, workload, and instruction of the class are all pretty good thanks to Ross, but you will be falling asleep anyway which is mostly the material's fault.

The only work outside of the midterm and final are 2 HW assignments, which are SQL practice, and the semester-long project has you building a full-stack application (Python/Flask) which is genuinely useful experience, especially earlier on in your CS career. There is also an option for a project without coding, though I do not know much about it except that it sounds more boring. Therefore, the homeworks are pretty useful. The midterm (15% of the grade) and final (40% of the grade) do ask a few SQL questions, but are mostly theoretical questions about DB management systems. The midterm and final averages were around a 60 for the midterm and a 45 for the final which are kind of crazy considering databases is not supposed to be a terribly difficult class. There is a policy where the final replaces the midterm but that doesn't really happen since the midterm is hard, but the final is an affront to God himself. Ross curves reasonably though, so if you are able to repress the anxiety your raw scores will undoubtedly give you, you'll be alright.

reviews.content:
This is genuinely one of the most defeating classes I have ever taken. I studied machine learning during my undergraduate degree and already have a fairly strong foundation in the subject, yet the questions in this course often feel unnecessarily difficult and completely disconnected from what is actually taught.

The average on the first exam was 22/60, with many students scoring around 9. At what point do results like these indicate a problem with the way the course is being assessed rather than with the students themselves?

The lectures teach one thing, the exams test something entirely different, and the homework assignments are another level of frustration. I have genuinely spent hours studying the material, only to encounter questions that seem almost impossible to approach using what we have been taught.

What makes this particularly frustrating is that Professor Verma is actually a good lecturer. He clearly understands the subject and can explain concepts well. However, the difficulty of his assessments feels excessive, almost as though the goal is to challenge students beyond reason rather than evaluate their understanding.

I rarely leave negative course evaluations, but I genuinely believe the MSAI department needs to reconsider making this particular course mandatory. Machine learning is an essential subject, but there is a difference between teaching rigorous ML and making students feel completely defeated despite putting in substantial effort.

I honestly do not know how a significant portion of the class is expected to pass at this rate. A challenging course should push students to learn, not make them question everything they already know. The assessment structure needs serious reconsideration.
reviews.workload:
The workload for this course is honestly excessive and incredibly draining. The homework assignments are extremely difficult and time-consuming, often requiring hours just to understand what the questions are asking, let alone solve them. There is a significant disconnect between the material covered in lectures and the level of difficulty expected in assignments and exams.

I understand that graduate-level machine learning should be rigorous, but the workload feels disproportionate to the learning outcomes. Instead of reinforcing concepts, the assignments often leave students frustrated, overwhelmed, and discouraged. Even with a prior background in machine learning, I have found myself spending unreasonable amounts of time on individual problems.

The course demands so much time that it becomes difficult to balance other classes, research commitments, and responsibilities. Challenging students is important, but the workload should be designed to promote learning rather than simply test how much frustration students can tolerate.

reviews.content:
Machine learning is a notoriously hard class and Tony Dear is a notoriously hard professor, so the combination was about as expected. The material was highly theoretical, though there was more application in HWs than with some other profs. The class was also structured better than other ML profs (in my opinion)

Take the pre requisites for this class seriously. 1) Linear algebra - Most test & theoretical HW questions were basically an exercise in how well you can APPLY linear algebra to prove theoretical ML concepts. 2) Statistics - prob/stats is fine but stat inference is really, really useful, especially for the first third of the class. It is certainly useful to know linear/multiple/logistic regression, ridge/lasso, and MLE before actually taking ML. 3) Multivariable calc - important for convex optimization (Lagrangian, gradients) and neural network back-propagation (partial derivatives/chain rule) 4) Optimization - MATH 2500 and IEOR 3609 are not strictly necessary but are pretty helpful for some parts of the course as well. If you are missing any of (1), (2), or (3), you will likely have a tough time. 

Dear explains the material very very well even if a little quickly. Like with his other classes, you walk out feeling like you learned an immense amount, even if your test grades do not reflect that. As with his other courses, the curve is very forgiving, which I think is a great reason to take this class... focus on learning this stuff and do not worry about your grade too much, it ends up being fine.
reviews.workload: There were 6 HW assignments and three midterms, all weighted equally. The HW assignments were not super long but were very difficult and would therefore take a while to do. I liked that the last few questions of every HW were applied, (ie. coding in Python with pytorch). There was no coding at all on tests so this just felt like a fun thing to do if you were interested in seeing the concepts your were learning in action and visualized, rather than something extra. The theoretical part of the HWs would be similar to test questions and would be very difficult. The first midterm was mostly pre req material and contained only a few, relatively easy ML concepts so it ended up being far easier than the following two midterms.

reviews.content:
Take Tony’s class if you want to learn ML in depth. At first, you may not fully understand why you need to learn so many mathematical concepts, because they are difficult and their purpose may not be immediately obvious. But as you go deeper into the field, you will gradually build your own knowledge map and realize how useful those concepts are.
This course mainly focuses on the mathematical foundations behind machine learning. Tony also tries to make the material more applicable by including coding questions that connect the theory to real-world applications.
That said, this course is hard. It is one of the hardest courses I have ever taken, so you should be prepared before taking it.
If you only want a good grade, you may want to take another professor’s version. If you want to learn something about ML but are not sure you can handle the workload, consider taking it PDF.

For a while, you were able to access the last year course page so you could look at the lecture slides ahead of time and try and figure out what was going on, but going to lectures was basically useless. The homework assignments took forever and constantly had issues, and I kept requesting regrades and got points back. The only part that seemed put together was Mihir and Pranav's office hours. If you can go to their office hours, it was soooooo much more helpful than the lectures. They also wrote the exams??? So going to their sessions was basically like hearing things that would be highly relevant for the exams. And they had these review sessions that were super nice and they kept bringing snacks which was nice. They care a lot. The other TAs kept referring me to their office hours, so I basically just asked questions on Ed and watched their reviews. Hopefully the class is taught better next semester but they have good TAs. FAQ:
#. Can you learn a lot in this course? Yes, but mostly on your own.
#. Is this the hardest CS course? No. It's hard, but acceptable.
#. Is this the worst CS course? Yes.
#. Is the instructor nice? Yes.
#. Does the instructor care about the course? Kind of. He only cares about lectures, everything else is left completely to the TAs.
#. Are lectures helpful for completing assignments? Slightly helpful. Slides mostly talk about Linux Kernel 20 years ago, but assignments are based on Linux Kernel 20 weeks ago.
#. Are TAs helpful? At least they tried. "We'll not help with debugging the code during OHs, because this is meant to be a hard class". In reality, they don't really know what's wrong with yours and, sometimes, their own, code.
#. Are TAs nice? Let me answer this question in a way that the TAs will answer your question: "The chances of us not trying to be nice is not necessarily high." Unlike other Columbia CS courses, we weren't given the opportunity to evaluate the TAs in the official course evaluation. Never expect to get a straightforward answer from any TAs.
reviews.workload:
FAQ:
#. Do assignments take lots of time? Yes.
#. Are assignments based? Mostly yes. They were originally designed by the legendary "Jae Woo Lee".
#. Are assignments' grading process based? No. Typically, what happens after students received their grades are: (1) Pressure TAs to release rubrics. (2) Carefully review the rubric and your solution. (3) Compare with the feedbacks you got. (4) Conclude that 85% of deductions are mistakes made by autograders or TAs. (5) Send regrade requests. (6) After a few days, an announcement will be made acknowledging large scale error when grading.
#. Are exams based? No. The exams were originally very based, because they were designed by Jae, the legend. Our TAs decided to "add their own color" to the exam, but they also claim that they are busy with their own exams and don't really have much time. Expect the median and average to be 45% and writing kernel code with pen and paper.
#. Are exams' grading process based? Can't draw a confident conclusion. For midterm, there were quite a few popular Ed posts complaining about the gradings. For finals, we didn't get to see our exams nor submit regrade requests. Perhaps our scores are directly sampled from a skewed Normal distribution? Who knows?

reviews.content:
Jason seems like a genuinely kind and well intentioned instructor, but the lecture content did not adequately prepare students for the exams. The exams were far too difficult given the level of instruction provided. They required a much deeper and more precise understanding than what was covered in class. He briefly went over portions of the Linux source code, yet the exams expected detailed, low level analysis far beyond those discussions. The exams were also extremely open ended, making it difficult to know whether you were even on the right track while answering. Given how challenging the homeworks already were, this made the exams feel unnecessarily punishing rather than a fair assessment of learning.

I expected this course to be challenging, but the homework assignments were far more punishing than anticipated. The average for nearly every homework being around a 40 is very concerning and should have been a clear signal that something was wrong with the structure of the course. Despite this, the exams were still made extremely difficult, which is hard to justify when the majority of students were already struggling to succeed on the assignments.

A major issue with the homeworks is that none of the individual parts provided any test cases, so there was no way to check whether you had implemented each part correctly before moving on. If you unknowingly failed an early part, you were essentially screwed for the remainder of the assignment. Since the homeworks often consisted of 12 interconnected parts worth 100 points total, a single mistake early on could cause everything else to fail and result in a zero.

There was also no reliable way to test your code in the same way it was graded. If your submission failed even the first hidden test case, you received a zero regardless of how much correct work you completed. Hours or days of work could be completely dismissed because of a single issue you had no way to detect. The homework specifications themselves were extremely unclear, with significant ambiguity between what was written in the spec and what was clarified later on Ed. Overall, the assignments and rubrics felt misaligned with the level of guidance provided. At the very least, partial credit should be awarded given the time and effort required. As it stands, the homework experience was the most frustrating I have had in a CS course at Columbia.

reviews.content: The hardest CS class in the department (if not in the country). Professor Nieh, is very warm and kind teacher. Knows the material inside out and has been teaching for the past 30 years. If you are taking OS, take it with him. He uses board and teaches the concept really good. He also goes over Linux code and tries to explain concept through code. What makes OS hard is: 1. it is a dense topic meant for 2 semesters so you are rushing through everything 2. Homework are intentionally made hard with verbose but unclear guidance for you to figure things out. They do it intentionally, so you go to office hours. Unless you understand the material, coding is a nightmare. You need to read ~1,000 lines of code every homework to code 10 lines (expect to write ~500 lines in C for some hws) - unless you want your code to deadlock. From my experience, I think they use a grading script, meaning that if your code don't compile you get 0, and their test cases are very hard (test, test, test your code). It is a team based assignment and choose your teams wisely. Unless this is your only class, have good team else you're going to suffer a lot. If you do not vibe with your teammates, switch on the next homework (they let you do that for every homework).  start early, in fact initial kernel compilation takes ~2 hours, so last minute work is impossible. Lecture is recorded with a policy that ~60 % attendance required to access the lecture recordings. No notes. However, Ed discussion is your best friend. Professor Nieh answers all questions on Ed. Start early, unless you understand your material nothing helps. You can use AI to explain concepts and cite it on your reference (but even then they do not help as much in fact it misleads you). the key is to learn it yourself. Unfortunately, reading books won't help as much than to attend lecture. His exams are fair, not tricky like AP, in fact if you attend lectures thoroughly and know what he is doing you can get 100 %, however each question holds more points than you think - they give partial credit unlike AP except for the hw (no parial credit).

Kostis is a very smart guy, and he will try his best to help you out during office hours, but I personally did not benefit from his teaching style. A good proportion of it is not his fault, and I wasn't able to understand him clearly for reasons beyond his control. However, he is relatively new to teaching OS and did not seem too familiar with the content or the homework. We had to rely heavily on the TAs of the class to resolve some of the finer questions, and entirely on the TAs for help on the assignments. Shoutout to them.

I did end up learning a good deal about operating systems, but in a bipolar way. On one hand, the assignments forced us to read line by line through source code on Bootlin. On the other, the lectures were super high level and rarely involved looking at OS code at all. So essentially there was a huge disconnect between the theory and the implementation of operating systems.

The content of the exams also seemed quite random and seemed to test more on OS trivia rather than kernel code, OS algorithm implementation, or HW knowledge. I don't know how else to describe it other than that some of the questions were "strange".

I've heard that Kostis is easier than Jason, and I feel like he will definitely get better as he teaches more, but as the class stands currently, I cannot recommend it.

reviews.content: A useful course in terms of the material being applied to software development and industry. However, the assessments in the course are very poor, requiring little effort, but with arbitrary outcomes. First, the quizzes are very detail-oriented and require quickly searching through the books - with lots of subtle tricks. Second, the project is graded quite harshly, for example in our class the average was 80 with 75 low and 85 high, lowering everyone's grade as it was a big part of the grade. So don't expect a great grade.

This class counts as a tech-light elective for the CS major. There is no coding involved at all.

This class goes over the basics Scrum, which is a team management style used in a lot of tech companies. There is a group project involved, and Tristan DOES NOT allow you to choose your own groups. If teaming up with potentially random strangers bothers you and you were planning on taking the class with a friend you know you can depend on, don't bother registering for it at all. The group project ended up being mostly fine, but the instructions were kind of vague and confusing. I took the class already and I still don't really know what they were looking for--I ended up writing a business plan that outlined the production of a make-believe product. We also had a group presentation.

We also have tedious, irritating weekly readings and quizzes. The content of the class is the exact same as the content in the book, so I stopped going to class (especially since it was from 8-10PM on a Thursday night). The questions are designed to trick you--Tristan usually writes questions by ripping quotes directly from the book and changing a single word, which makes it very easy to trip up. His insistence on this style of evaluation shows how insecure he is: he is afraid that people don't take his class seriously, so he makes his quizzes difficult to ace so we are forced to take it seriously. The readings were long--if you actually did them and took the careful notes you needed for the quiz, it would probably take about six hours.

The content was interesting from an optimizing workflow perspective, but overall painstaking and not a good use of time.

This is a CS course but there is no need to code.

3. Essential Scrum: A Practical Guide to the Most Popular Agile Process (Addison-Wesley Signature Series) by Kenneth S. Rubin
4. A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK® Guide)–Fifth Edition
The lectures covered mostly on the 3rd book: Essential Scrum.
Other books are verbose and quite boring.

Some events in the lectures are likely to invoke your childhood but those events have nothing to do with grade.

There is a project proposal & presentation done in groups at the end of the semester.
The presentation is likely to take a lot of time but the effort you made will probably be meaningless.
Although there are given grading rubrics (copied directly from the last semester without changing the dates in the document), the final scores are quite subjective and the grading rubrics don't really give you the proportion of what item should be covered more in the proposal/presentation.
There was a voting on team presentations but there was no explicit announcement about whether this will affect the grade. The result was not publicly announced after the grade was released.
Usually, team presentations are divided into two weeks and teams in the 2nd week will do much better on the presentation because they can learn from the 1st week.
You can get a good grade if you are in the right group even if you seldom go to classes or attend group meetings.

Find good friends that will notify you which class needs to sign up or sign up for you.

Most quiz answers are not given at the end of semester so it is hard to learn from your mistake.

There is a high probability that you get something around or over 90 before the final proposal/presentation score is released.
The distribution of the final proposal/presentation is
high: 90
mean: around 80
low: 65
so there is a high probability that it will lower your score.

Part of the issue was that a large portion of the class didn't really have the mathematical maturity necessary for this course, and she would get bogged down answering basic questions and then have to rush through material. She got better at this (i.e. stopped answering stupid questions) as the semester went on, but it remained frustrating throughout.

Homework assignments were well-designed. Fernando (the TA) was a real stickler for rigor, and I definitely learned to be more careful about writing up proofs by the end of the semester. Midterm (in class) and final (take home) were both trivial; I don't know what the final average was, but due to the aforementioned mathematical maturity problem midterm scores were shockingly low.

As a side note, this can be a great class even if you're not specifically interested in security. I was in learning theory at the same time, and my final project for that class relied on a bunch of cryptographic hardness assumptions---this is about a lot more than secret codes.

reviews.content:
Augustin is a very enthusiastic, friendly guy. He goes out of his way to encourage people to speak during class, even as far as to buy apples before class and give them to people who raise their hand and participate in any way. You can respond to one of his questions correctly, incorrectly, you can ask him to repeat the question, you can ask "may I please get an apple", as long as some sound passes between your lips he will give you an apple.

This class was much more theoretical than I anticipated. Augustin attempts to summarize papers on sociology, graph theory, social psychology or other topics related to models of large-scale social behavior. Some of the models make sense, for others he makes no attempt to prove that they reflect real-life trends; they simply seem like one person's interpretation of a complicated phenomenon.

After giving a bit of intuition for the motivation for the model of the day, he dives into a heavily mathematical proof for all sorts of bounds relating to the proof which can quickly become overwhelming. He often lingers on finishing up algebra for longer than necessary, but then makes overestimates our knowledge of certain statistical / linear algebraic theorems and rushes through parts of the proof that seem to fly over most people's heads.

The homeworks usually involve taking the ideas covered in class and generalizing them and proving those generalizations, which was almost impossible to do on one's own. Nothing is googleable.

As other people have said, Augustin is very disorganized. His homeworks are hodgepodges of older homeworks along with new questions hastily written with minimal proofreading. The data challenges took a while to put together, and when they came out we had relatively little time to prepare our setups. The TAs did not fully understand a lot of the material, and we would often have to "learn together" during office hours. For a 4995, this class felt more like a 6998 (which I believe it used to be).

reviews.content:
This class is a mixed bag.

The biggest positive is that this is probably the most practically useful ML-related course at Columbia. If you take the time to really understand the material, you will come away with a solid grasp of how modern NLP systems and LLMs work. The course covers classic NLP topics like language modeling, tagging, parsing, semantics, machine translation, summarization, question answering, and dialogue systems, but the second half focuses heavily on neural network architectures, including RNNs, attention, transformers, BERT, GPT, RAG, and RLHF. The homework assignments are in Python/PyTorch, and they are genuinely useful for understanding how neural networks are actually implemented. 

In my opinion, this class is much more valuable than the standard ML class if your goal is practical understanding. The ML class is more theoretical and only briefly touches on neural networks. NLP gives you a much better feel for how modern ML systems are used in practice.

The downside is the lectures. Daniel Bauer seems like a nice guy, but I did not think he was an effective lecturer. He tries to cover way too much material in each class and often moves through complicated neural network ideas and architectures as if everyone has already seen them before. If you want to really understand what is going on, you will need to do a lot of self-study. This is especially true because many of the architectures and techniques are relatively new, and not everything has a clean theoretical explanation.

The recommended Goldberg textbook is pretty good, especially for the neural network parts. I would read the sections relevant to each lecture. If you are new to neural networks, the 3Blue1Brown videos are also very helpful. I would focus on the textbook and professor-provided implementation notes for the homeworks. I would mostly skip the extra papers and articles unless you are especially interested, because they are usually not the best way to learn the core ideas.

My recommendation is to watch the lectures with AI ready to explain things, and pause often. Take good notes, especially for the neural network and transformer material. Do the homeworks yourself. Use AI only to debug, explain confusing code, or help with PyTorch syntax. The homeworks are where you actually learn how the ideas are used, so do not waste that opportunity.

Overall, I think taking the class is a good idea, but not because the lectures are great. I would recommend it because the material is extremely relevant, the assignments are useful, and the course gives you a practical foundation in modern NLP and neural networks if you are willing to teach yourself the parts that are not explained well in lecture.
reviews.workload:

The homeworks are manageable, and the exams are very doable if you make good note sheets, understand the homeworks, and do the theoretical practice problems.

This is an easy course if you only want to do around average, which is roughly an A-. If you actually care about understanding the material deeply, expect to spend a lot more time: probably around five hours per lecture between pausing, taking notes, looking things up, and reading outside material. If you do that consistently, you should be in a strong position to get an A. An A+ is also realistic if you stay on top of the material, since roughly the top 10% of the class gets one.

reviews.content:
This is definitely a lighter class for padding your GPA. Junfeng is extremely kind, but his lectures are mundane and mediocre. In fact, all of his slides are copied verbatim from an edX course by UC Berkeley. The same applies for the programming assignments on Codio. Junfeng says you can qualify for extra credit that can bump you to an A+ if you attend class, but this wasn't worth it for most people. Since the class was at 8:40, the classroom was usually a ghost town after the first month. The lectures are recorded, but they're very loosely related to the assignments.

The only value comes from the semester long group project, where the class breaks off into teams of 4 to develop a SaaS solution using Ruby on Rails. It's imperative that you find competent teammates ASAP. Don't be afraid to sell yourself on the Ed discussion board—if you have prior internship/work experience at FAANG/M7/HFT or any other prestigious firm, then leverage the hell out of it! Unless you already have friends in the class, this is the only way to ensure that you'll find likeminded teammates. The project is 50% of your grade and you'll be stuck with your team for the whole time, so choose wisely.

Overall, I'd recommend if you need an easy class to fill a COMS 41xx requirement. If you just want to learn Ruby on Rails, you might as well go through the edX course on your own time.

reviews.workload: More assignments in the first half of the semester and it tones down after that. Uses javascript. No exams, just homework (not weekly) and a final project. Most exciting/fun part is live coding

reviews.content: Computational Sound was definitely a class on the easier side, and Mark is a really good professor who always answers my questions during his office hours really thoroughly. Although I loved the projects I worked on for that class and really put in the effort into it, I didn’t learn as much as I wanted to from the lectures and feel like I could have learned the information taught on my own.
reviews.workload: Easy workload - Assignments 60%, Participation 10%, Final project 30%

reviews.content: One of my favorite classes at Columbia. Expected small workload going in, and honestly did not take much to succeed in the class. 2 in-class quizzes that if you watch the weekly assigned films and understand the historical context you'll get 10/10, weekly 400-500 word reviews of required films that you only need to do six out of twelve, and final project with a group or a 10 page essay. Professor Qian is so easygoing and kind, very understanding, and truly understands the student experience. TAs are also very helpful and nice! Also learned a lot about Asian history and culture, had a director as guest lecturer, and caught up on some famous films I haven't watched but have always wanted to. Would recommend this class to anyone, good luck getting off the waitlist.
reviews.workload: Grading was very fair, usually done by TAs. They also gave comments and feedback that was super helpful.

reviews.content: Very interesting topics and films. Professor Qian is very nice! Highly recommend!
reviews.workload: 2 quizes, in total 6 weekly film discussion post, midterm paper, final project

reviews.content:
Took this because it was a 4-point global core that met once a week and discussed movies. Sounds chill, and it was. Throughout the semester it was unclear how tough the TA's would be, but turns out they were light graders. This is either because they graded everything at the end of the semester and got tired of it and just passed out A's, or they truly believed we deserved them. Regardless, easy A.

We covered a movie every week, which we are responsible for viewing in designated 'viewing party' on Thursdays 7-9pm, (unless you have an excused absence). During class, Professor Qian gave a 1-hour lecture on the history of the Asian culture that the movie covers so that we have further context, followed by a TA-led discussion about scenes from the movie. It ended up being the same 3-4 students talking about their interpretations of the scenes, followed by long monologues by the TAs who just liked to hear themselves speak. Also, I'm pretty sure no one did the readings or watched the additional clips or really even showed up to the film screenings (which, by the way, were supposed to be mandatory... but in a class of ~50, I never saw more than 12 people there). 

1 midterm paper, which was just an analysis of 2 films (4-6 pages, easy). 1 midterm project, where you get into a group of 1-5 students and recreate a scene from one of the films. This project was meant to recreate the filming process, from staging, to considering mis-en-scene, acting, point of view, etc. The film clip was 5-6 minutes and was completed in one saturday for my group. For the final, you had the option to write a 12-page paper or to create your own shortfilm, using the techniques we learned in class. My group and I chose to do this, as none of us wanted to write a 12-page paper, and because filming was pretty fun. We wrote a super loose plot, discussed it with the TA who told us everything to include that she wanted to see, and filmed it all in 1 saturday. Putting it all together took a little longer than the midterm project, but thats because this was 15 minutes. 

This class was interesting, and super easy. I highly recommedn if youre looking for 4 credits, an easy A, to learn about east asian cinema and how it was influenced by other historical factors and especially Hollywood, or just want to make a short film. I recommend it, but beware, it is not the most engaging lecture you will sit through.
reviews.workload:
5 response posts on the movies of our choice (500 words following a prompt, graded check minus, check, or check plus),
1 midterm paper (4-6 pages on 2 films, following a prompt of choice)
1 midterm project (recreate a scene from one of the films, 5 minute clip)
1 final paper OR project (create your own short film, 15 minutes)

reviews.content: This is a very interesting and engaging course that could be used for Global Core requirement. If you're looking for an enjoyable Global Core course or some intro film course, this course would probably fulfill your needs. If you're somewhat knowledgeable on East Asian history, either China, Japan, or Korea, it would be helpful. Background knowledge on film could be useful, but not necessary. The class covers East Asian films from the early 20th century up to the early 21st century, from silent black and white films to modern Hollywood movies. As for class structure, we meet once a week for lecture and there's weekly movie screening, which apparently was optional, but now required. Professor Qian is very nice and approachable, and she works really hard to make the course as enjoyable as it could be. The only downside was that it felt like announcements and grading were often rushed, delayed until the very last minute, but I'm pretty sure it difficult to find a class which isn't (at least that was the case for me).
reviews.workload:
Attendance; lectures and weekly screening (15%)
Weekly posting assigned on required films, but you only need to complete only 5 of them (20%)
Midterm Paper on film of your choice (20%)
Video group assignment; you get to recreate a scene from a film of your choice, or create original short film 8-10 minutes (10%)
Final Essay or Creative Project; you either write a paper covering multiple films or do something similar to video group assignment. We were also given the option of video essay (35%)

reviews.content: Going into this class I had so much hope it would be amazing due to the gold nugget on CULPA. I would say I was overconfident. The biggest challenge is the total lack of practical, structured instruction. In class, there are no slides, and the materials the professor shares after class aren't even his own and rarely align with his lectures. To make matters worse he teaches a completely different method for solving every problem than what will be on the test. The test ALWAYS align with the textbook, so why does he spend our class time teaching his own personal shortcut we cannot even use? This class has been an incredibly frustrating experience. If you rely on structured learning, DO NOT TAKE. He is a wonderful person, but a very unstructured prof.

reviews.content: His lectures are quite boring and confusing, but his slides are excellent and cover all the content so no need to open the textbook. Both exams are very similar to the practice tests and he clearly wants students to succeed. I would definitely recommend taking his class, easy A.
reviews.workload: Light workload, never did reading because slides covered all topics and one assignment a week which takes around 10-30 mins.

reviews.content: He certainly isn't a bad person (anymore, I guess?) but he's definitely not the best lecturer. He does seem a bit nervous, and he definitely stumbles here and there, but he's pretty kind. I recommend going to lectures anyways, but you can also self-study the material (he uploads slides to Courseworks before every lecture). I knew people who only took notes to stay awake in class. We used a free online textbook—his slides are the EXACT same material, so if you need a more in-depth explanation, you can refer to it. I'd say the exams are more in-depth than the psets and what we cover in class. Take Prof. Dye's class if you have a foundation in Econ and can self study. Recitations were sort of helpful.

reviews.content: Lowkey a very boring class, concepts are quite simple (especially if you have previous econ experience) and he's not a particularly engaging lecturer. Would def recommend going to recitations (though they're not mandatory), the TAs were better at explaining concepts and answering questions than him. He posts a sample exam for both the midterm and the final, and both tests are almost exactly like the sample
reviews.workload: Roughly 1 assignment per week, midterm exam, final exam

reviews.content: The worse thing of his class is the real exam never match what he test about. The next worse thing is that is explanation of definitions aren't helpful at all and sometimes if you try to understand his explanation, you will NEVER be able to grasp that.... If you have other choice, then don't take his class. However, he's a kind person.
reviews.workload: The workload is okay but I won't say it's easy A

reviews.content: She has a lot of passion which illuminated the course content and also was able to explain very complex subjects in simple terms that made it easy to understand; that being said I found the course as well as the prof slightly unorganized and unpredictable. The final paper is completely on ur own without any sort of formal guidance, and you are expected to have an idea of ur research topic from the moment of the first day of classes. But the grading is fair
reviews.workload: Varies a lot depending on how the structure of the course changes; overall not high

reviews.content: Lalith is possibly the worst professor on campus, and certainly the least helpful.   As others have stated, he is disgustingly arrogant and pretentious-- His head is so far up his bum, I don't know how he can breathe. Spending a couple of hours a week at a round table with him was torture. He was unapproachable and condescending and didn't even seem to enjoy teaching.  Most classes consisted of discussions on the readings and related theories. The books were very interesting and the course should have been an amazing experience but Lalith managed to ruin it. If you can avoid it, do NOT take a class with this excuse of a professor.
reviews.workload: Reading required a couple of hours a week.

reviews.content:
i don't get the john hype. he is fine, but his lectures often seem very uninspired. he's so focused on teaching the math behind the concepts that i feel like you lose some of the theory or what makes economics actually interesting. basically the course was very boring even though i like labor economics. 

clearly i am in the minority though. there's no doubt he's good at explaining things.
reviews.workload: midterm, final, group project/presentation

reviews.content:
Lalith is definitely a fan of his own research, and prone to telling us about each of his studies and particular areas of interest several times without remembering entire half-lectures on it before.

But still. He makes himself very available, encourages discussion in class (although it is true that he isn't too kind to people who get it wrong, so just learn to shake it off). He genuinely loves the topic, and it's obvious. His lectures are clear, he treats students with respect, and there was a definite camaraderie - this is what I came to Barnard for. I think he's pretty funny, too.
reviews.workload: Nine sporadic ungraded problemsets (not bad at all), straightforward midterm and final. We also had a mini 2 page half-paper during reading week that some people complained about, but was really more interesting and philosophical than difficult although it could have been better timed.

reviews.content:
She's not the worst but she's far from the best professor you can have. Take her class if you don't have better options. I think in most aspects she was alright. I found her lectures boring and unengaging, but I know that wasn't the sentiment across the class. Some people really liked her lecture style and thought it was engaging. The workload for her class I would say is very reasonable. There are 3 homework each spaced out with decent time in between and not too long. The GIS portion of the homework can be time-consuming but the ERC workshop videos are helpful enough to get anyone through it without much trouble. There's one midterm and one final. Both tests are online and she gives the entire day for students to complete it. The tests have two portions: an MC portion and a written portion. Her MC questions can be difficult but overall both exams are passable with a decent amount of studying. And there is a group presentation+paper at the end of the semester on a topic of your choice. There is an overwhelming amount of reading for the class but you can get by just skimming a few of them. 
The biggest problem with her class is that what she teaches in class is very different from what shows up in HW and her tests. She barely covers math examples in her lectures yet 90% of her HW and tests require math. The math examples she does cover in class hardly help. There are a few of them where she does the math on paper and posts it on slides, good luck trying to read her handwriting. The math itself is not difficult math but you will have to teach the concepts to yourself because Professor Archibong will not teach you it. The second problem with her class is that there is no TA for the class to ask for question+guidance and Professor Archibong is the single worst person to go for clarification. If you ask for clarification often time she will tell you to post it on the discussion board instead of clarifying for you even if the clarification is very specific to you. This especially becomes frustrating during the group project when you might need some very specific guidance.
reviews.workload: 3 HW, 1 Midterm, 1 Final (Cumulative), A group paper+presentation on a topic of your choice

reviews.content: Professor Gertler adapts as a teacher. Many of the bad reviews are an exaggeration. She is a very conceptual teacher and has improved as a teacher so much the past semester that I have been taking in her class. I struggled in the beginning because I did not understand her phrasing, but once you begin to understand it, it truly helps the way you understand the world of economics. She is as sweet as candy and if you want a class that is not too hard to get an A, this is the class to take.
reviews.workload: About one problem set per two lectures, 2 midterms, one final (not cumulative and is the same weight as the other midterms)

reviews.content: Lectures were sometimes confusing, but he's overall a nice guy/helpful professor. The TA, Joel, is wonderful & hosts very helpful office hours. The problem sets are optional but very similar to the format of his in class quizzes & exams.

reviews.content: Overall I did not enjoy this course. He is not an engaging lecturer and is extremely repetitive. The one thing I will say is that the homework assignments prepare you well for the in class quizzes. However, they don't prepare you super well for the midterm or final. Both exams include multiple-choice sections and a "discussion question". He does not give any practice with the discussion questions throughout the course.
reviews.workload: Midterm exam 30%, final exam 46%, quizzes 24% (4 grades at 6% each) -- you take 5 quizzes and drop your lowest score. You get docked points if you get a multiple-choice question wrong, but you don't lose any points if you leave a question blank. Annoying policy he says is aimed to prevent people from blindly guessing. Just have to do the assignments (not graded, just practice problems) to prepare well for the quizzes.

reviews.content: I love Prof. Williams. Out of all the econ classes I have taken, this class has been the most engaging, and I got lucky as most people in my class were eager to participate. Since the class size is smaller, it feels easier to share thoughts during lecture. Although this class does not require econometrics, Prof. Williams shows slides about it somewhat frequently but still emphasizes that you don't need to know it so much (I don't think I ever applied it in assignments/exams). I really loved this class and recommend it!
reviews.workload: Assignments were like PSETs, and were graded mostly to completion. I think there was only 1 TA responsible for grading so I will say it took a while. It definitely helps to be an active participant in class as I feel that it improved my grade even though my exam results were just above average.

reviews.content:
To be honest, Health Econ would not be one of the electives that would come to mind when fulfilling the econ requirement, but let this be a sign for you to take it with Prof Williams. This is one of the easiest economics elective you'll find: light workload and easy content. Course content covers demand of health, the US insurance industry, race and medicine, algorithms in medicine, and more. The class is structured really well with clear and concise lecture slides as resource. PSets are also very doable, just refer to examples in slides/textbook. Got an A in this course despite spending less than half the time compared to other econ courses, while also learning so much on the economic side of the healthcare system.

All in all, Prof. Williams is just a kind soul, fun guy, and genuinely passionate in his field. His lectures are engaging and were very helpful in office hours. Highly recommend taking a class with him!
reviews.workload: 2 midterms (25% each, one of it is take-home), 20% group policy memo, 10% group presentation, 20% assignment (4 PSets, drop one). 3 hours max per week on assignments and readings - longer in the final few weeks when doing research for group presentation/policy memo.

reviews.content: Genuinely the best! Take at least one class with him before you graduate. He is able to explain difficult concepts in a way that makes them seem easy and digestible.

reviews.content: Maria Lozano is the best. She's very knowledgable about immigration issues related to Latin America, and has a particular area of expertise in bilingual education, which is what the education policy portion of the class is about. I'd say what is best about Professor Lozano, however, is how supportive she is. It can be hard to learn a new language, and Professor Lozano is very encouraging for anyone who wants to learn, no matter their skill level, and she is always approachable during office hours. I'm going into continuing my spanish education with a level of optimism and confidence that is completely do to her.

reviews.content: I usually don't write reviews, but this class was truly an eye-opening experience. If you are interested in going into the legal field at all, even if non-environmental, I'd recommend this class. Dana is truly an amazing teacher. She cares about her students and wants everyone to become more engaged citizens. I became less apathetic and more inspired to utilize law in order to fight the climate crisis. We learned how to read and brief cases in a way that we'd learn in our first year at law school. We go through and analyze environmental law cases and how their decisions affect the outcomes of future cases. A large portion of the class is learning how to do legal research through legal databases.

She is always open to questions and OH appointments. She took us to Joe Coffee after class if we wanted to have follow-up discussions. The readings can be a lot some weeks, but reasonable considering we only meet once a week. There is a class project with check-points along the semester, where we can get feedback before the final is turned in. Exercises and midterms were reasonable and explained beforehand. Mock brief presentation to judges as the final.

reviews.content: The only required text for this class was the Norton Anthology of American Literature 1820-1865, and I believe the bookstore had used copies to purchase. This was truly one of the most amazing classes I have taken at Barnard thus far. I took it at 8:40am and was expecting the content to be a bit dry (due to the nature of the readings) however it was anything but. Professor Zarour Zarzar showed up every morning excited about the readings and with a whole bunch of valuable knowledge to share. It takes a lot to get me out of bed for an 8:40 class, but I think I was only absent one time. Genuinely, this class made me feel like I could study English if I wanted and taught me a lot about a really significant era of history as well. Additionally, it was a lecture class but he always facilitated discussion while also keeping us moving pretty quick through content. Definitely recommend!!!
reviews.workload: About 50-200 pages of reading a week. Some weeks where novels were assigned were responsible for the higher end of this range, but I think that is pretty typical of any English class. One group project video, one midterm, one essay, and one final project. Other than that everything was in-class.

reviews.content: I should start by saying that I think Professor Gordis is a kind, flexible, and dedicated professor. Her lectures and the course itself was incredibly thorough and it's very clear that she cares a lot about the readings and the students in the class. That being said, this class was miserable for me. Her lectures are tedious and difficult to get through. They consist of obscenely long powerpoints (like 60-80 slides per reading) with just giant blocks of quotes from the texts we had to read. She reads the quotes out in their entirety, which kind of defeats the purpose of struggling through the readings (of which there are MANY) and doesn't provide any visual aid for the complex topics that she's trying to illustrate. It's clear she's read reviews that complained about how she just lectures at us, so every couple of slides, she'll stop and ask the most unthoughtprovoking question ever: what does everyone think of this? This class would be a lot more bearable if it was a discussion but for some inexplicable reason she insists on lecturing at us.
reviews.workload: Professor Gordis also assigns the most absurd amount of readings that I've ever seen in a class. The course meets twice a week and you should expect to have at least 3 hours of difficult 19th century literature to get through for each class, sometimes more. I gave up trying to do the readings halfway through the course which made the class even more unbearable. It is a fairly easy class to do well in (although I haven't taken the cumulative, 3 hour long final). There's only one 6-8 page essay which is due at the end of the semester. She also uses a strange online platform called Yellowdig so that she can track everyone's response posts and participation in something she calls a commonplace book, which are basically just mini responses. Professor Gordis is nice and really dedicated -- I wish that I could read as much as she thought we could read. But this class was the bane of my existence this semester -- take it only if you are super into 19th century literature or need the literature before 1900 requirement for the English major.

reviews.content:
Have to disagree with those that believe Gordis to be cruel or overly-harsh; her tough grading (with always the offer of a thorough review if turned in a week early that can be rewritten and turned in!) improved my writing more than any other single class I have taken. She was always willing to discuss texts further outside of class, or make suggestions for outside research. If you are a serious Americanist, she will help you more than you know. Yes, she is not always easy to get ahold of, and may seem rigid in her scheduling, but she's crazy busy and simply expects students to respect her time.

Yes, the class is a lot of work, but the weekly writing etc helps you engage with often dense or less exciting texts--let's be honest, America doesn't begin its literary golden age until the end of the this course, and really, most of the great writers are in the 20th. Despite that, she provides a number of ways to approach the text and find meaning (except The Last of the Mohicans, fuck that book, I mean I get why its there but GOD I hate it). 

Basically, if you really care about understanding American lit, and why we are the way that we are, take a class with Gordis.
reviews.workload: The most I've ever had--average 350 pages reading a week, 10 short blog posts over semester, two papers, intensive exam involving identification of works and short essays.

reviews.content: I felt that this class was neither spectacular nor awful.  Professor Gordis is really sweet in class but her lectures are difficult to follow because they don't seem to have any logical progression from start to finish.  There's always a lot of flipping back in forth in really large texts and it's easy to get lost.  She'll also cite a page number and then immediately start reading from some undisclosed and random point on the page, so by the time you figure out where she's reading from she's already moved on to commentary and you've missed half of what she said.  I really enjoyed the blog element of this course.  There is no word count minimum for the blog posts (I think they tended to be about 200 words), so it's easy to get these done and the posts actually really helped to make the material more interesting and get people engaged.
reviews.workload: Weekly reading, weekly blog posts (she provides "provocations" to which students respond), two 5-6 page papers, and final.

reviews.content:
Mean, sarcastic, arrogant, draconian, Harvard-obsessed, overly impressed with herself.

Prof. Gordis will shoot down comments in class because she disagrees with the strength of the adjectives one uses. Her lectures are clearly rehearsed and  it is difficult for her to deviate, as class discussions often necessitate. 

Office hours are sparse and unworkable for a student schedule: she once offered me 8am on a Friday, take it or leave it. Go to office hours and she'll sit there with her arms crossed like a smug weasel. The only time she's nice is if you can get her talking about her undergrad days at Harvard, twenty-five years ago. 

I'm an English major, and I am glad that Gordis was not my first exposure to literature at Barnard. Absolutely terrible experience.
reviews.workload: Very heavy. I'm an English major so I expected this, but this class was ridiculous. Weekly blog posts plus comments and "provocations". Reading about 300 pages per class. Two six page essays (do-able, but do not expect to get above a B- on either). One absolutely absurd AP-style 3-hour final with two hour-long essay sections and quote identifications. Take another American Lit class, or take it at Columbia.

reviews.content: Had him for critical writing and lowk would not recommend if you want the normal version of this class. With him it was very chill and not a lot of work, especially considering it was a 4 credit class. Did not really learn anything new tbh.
reviews.workload: SOOO light. 3 essays. Readings include poems, one play (Macbeth by Shakespeare), and one novel (Jazz by Toni Morrison).

reviews.content: My favorite professor so far. Just communicate with her and you should be fine grade-wise. I had a lot going on when I took her class and wasn't able to get assignments in on time etc but she was very kind about it and remained approachable. She's a bit strict in the sense that she will point out small errors but she also praises all the good parts of your essay; if you genuinely want to refine your writing (which you probably need in the long term for any discipline) I would highly recommend her course. The readings were all enjoyable and thought-provoking
reviews.workload: Completely manageable, one discussion board post per week and 4 essays

reviews.content: I'll be candid here... she is the most cynical and draconian grader I have ever had here at Barnard. If I hadn't taken other English courses I would be dissuaded from majoring in English because this lady has a way of discouraging students through her harsh grading style and "reverse psychology" method employed in class. You can tell she uses reading and work as an escapist activity from socializing with people, because she lacks the empathy and ability to connect with her students. If you are doing poorly, please remember that your proficiency as a writer is not reflected by the grades she gives out. She is an intellectual snob who is unhappy with the card she has been dealt with in life and takes it out on her students.
reviews.workload: HEAVY. Weekly reading responses... and they aren't casual, she expects an essay as well as 5 harshly graded papers.

reviews.content:
I started out loving this class but I DO NOT feel that way now!  Spiegel is unorganized.  While the other sections were reading literary favorites and writing essays, we were discussing memory the ENTIRE semester.  We read books, articles, and watched movies about memory and history.  It seems to be her expertise which she then applies to every course that she teachers - whether it is this course or a film course, I have a feeling that the syllabi are very similar.  
We were supposed to have weekly courseworks postings but she stopped those because she kept forgetting to put up prompts and questions for us to discuss. She didn't assign us any essays to write until halfway through the semester so we had to rush in 3 essays instead of having them spread out thanks to Spiegel's unorganized and chaotic nature.
And then is the grading.  It took her a VERY long time to give us our grades for the first paper.  We were graded harshly and everyone in the class said that they were surprised by her harsh and rather rude comments and grades.  This could partly be because it was our first grade all semester and she told us that we were all doing better than we ended up doing on the paper.  On the same note, I asked her if I should rewrite a draft of my essay and she said it was not necessary and that  I would do very well on the paper.  Well, she lied.  I did not do very well and it is not just that I have oddly high standards.  I did not improve from the paper before - instead she gave me the same grade slash the grade one portion of a grade higher (ex. B/B+ or B+/A-).  
In the end, I DO NOT recommend this class because I am unhappy with the way Professor Spiegel handled the structure of the course and the grading.  She was fake, unorganized, and unnecessarily harsh.  If she wants us to improve and learned from our past assignments, space them out throughout the semester and not squish them into the last two months.
reviews.workload:
About a book or movie a week with the occasional article.  If you are smart and a good BSer, you can get away without completing a book or two.
Weekly courseworks postings until she forgets to put up the question for too many weeks in a row
Essays. We had 3 because she didn't assign us any until halfway through but I think she originially said she would assign 5.  They were other random written assignments on the syllabus that she did not assign us to do

reviews.content:
This was one of the best classes I've taken so far. The syllabus is amazing. There's A LOT (too much) of reading for the class, but it's all really fundamental (Plato, Aristotle, Nietzsche, Shakespeare, Jane Austen, Marx, and a lot more). The works we read always seemed to be useful for all of my other classes.  After this class you just won't ever look at theory/ aesthetics the same way again.

The syllabus is challenging, but Stefan was a great guide. He was always patient in going over tough points (and incredibly generous when it came to office hours). His enthusiasm for the material was infectious: by the end of the semester I could barely believe I had done all the reading (well almost all of the reading).

After this class you'll really feelmuch better prepared for your other English classes.  The syllabus and the professor are great!
reviews.workload: Insane. But totally worthwhile. And from what I hear not that much more than other sections of the class.

reviews.content:
I’m writing to pay tribute to this incredible man. This class has been a mind-blowing, life-changing engagement with psychoanalytical theories, which are often stigmatized (alongside literary theories like Saussure). The course reexamines overused terms like ego, uncanny, castration, etc., within the contexts in which they were originally written, pushing you to grasp their nuanced meanings in psychoanalysis. 

More than merely using psychoanalysis as a lens to understand literature, this class explored how the two disciplines inform and enrich each other. We specifically analyzed To the Lighthouse alongside the confluence and deviations between psychoanalysis and modernism. Other texts included Act III of Hamlet, The Sandman by E.T.A. Hoffmann, “Funes, His Memory” by Jorge Luis Borges, “A Farewell" and "The Widower" by Arthur Schnitzler, A Report to an Academy and The Hunger Artist by Kafka, Ex Machina, “We Can Remember It For You Wholesale" by Philip K. Dick, and “Going to Meet the Man” by James Baldwin.

The psychoanalytic texts we studied included Freud's Three Case Histories, Civilization and Its Discontents, The Interpretation of Dreams, Repression, and "A Note Upon the ‘Mystic Writing-Pad’"; Lacan's “The Mirror Stage as Formative of the I Function as Revealed in Psychoanalytic Experience” from Écrits; Powers of Horror by Julia Kristeva; and “When Our Lips Speak Together” by Luce Irigaray.

I cannot express just how much I love Professor Gorelick. I’ve been in his classes since I was a sophomore, and he is the most intelligent, kind, and competent person I’ve ever met. It’s not just the scope and depth of his classes but also his eloquence in communicating and synthesizing complex, abstract ideas in logical, coherent, and seamless ways, which shows just how well he knows his stuff. I had to transcribe many of his lectures because they were downright brilliant. As I review my notes, the logic becomes clearer over time, simply because of how breathtakingly methodical his lectures were.

As an educator, his class objectives and standards are equally meticulous. The way he designs exams and his slideshow presentations (and if you’re an English major, you’ll understand how valuable and rare well-crafted slides are) always made me feel like I’ve precisely reached the class objectives at every phase. His dedication to providing thorough and thoughtful resources is unmatched.

He genuinely cares about his students, connects with their ideas efficiently. He is always open-minded, and welcomes refreshing and intellectual dialogues. Every time I visit his office hours, he has precise questions and insights that accurately pinpoint areas for improvement. I’m consistently amazed by his refined intellect and by how funny, approachable, and loving he is.

The intellectual load and amount of readings were manageable but demanded genuine engagement with the concepts and theories. Despite the complexity of the course materials, Professor Gorelick made the process very entertaining and enriching, so don't worry if the readings and theories seemed daunting at first glance.
reviews.workload: A dream journal consisting of 12 dreams, with your own interpretations for 6 of them based on chain of associations; 5 discussion posts between 100–300 words; 2 exams; 3 pop reading quizzes (which require a general read-through of the readings. No difficult questions about concepts, just basic information provided by the texts). As long as you keep up with what is presented in class and maintain a general understanding of the readings, you'll do fine on the exams. They are more educational than evaluative.

reviews.content: Nathan maintains the best balance between academic rigorousness and having fun in class. As long as you really have something to say rather than trying to evade producing and engaging in good ideas, it's gonna be an easy A. He's still young in his thirties so he knows how to be witty and funny in class, and he cares and understands students and treats students like good friends. I'd highly recommend, he's just sooooooo nice and super chill.
reviews.workload:
· 3~4 discussion posts, as long as you devote some effort and have decent ideas in them, he'll mark as A and complete
· 3 concept paper (much like reflect papers),  2-3 page papers, demonstrate your efforts to understand some of the difficult ideas included in one of the readings in three of the modules. Each one worth 5 points, but the lowest he gives on those papers would be about 4.6
· Salon discourse in which you prepare a staged conversation with one or two other students. As long as you reflect and discuss ideas talked about in class, easy A
· 8-10 page final research paper (need two outside sources, engage in only one of the readings in any of the modules)

reviews.content: I didn't really know what to expect from this class since I hadn't taken a creative writing workshop before, but this class blew me away. Professor Batuman is incredibly smart, interesting, empathetic, and overall a lovely person, writer, and professor. She assigned readings to us each week based on what she specifically thought would be interesting and relevant for our writing. Every class we discussed the readings and workshopped two pieces by our peers.
reviews.workload: The assignments were: weekly readings, preparing discussion questions about the readings for two weeks, two 8-15 page creative writing pieces (but the second could be a revision of the first), artist dates (doing something for your inner artist about every other week by yourself), and morning pages a few times a week (writing three pages without stopping)

reviews.content: Love the prof, first few classes were lectures to contextualize baudelaire/rimbaud and their respective literary work, then became analysis of selected poems by each author (1 by alphonse de lamartine, some by baudelaire, some by rimbaud, 1 on mallarme but didn't particularly get deep into his work).
reviews.workload:
1 midterm paper, 1 final paper, 1 presentation
re: the presentation --- about half way into the semester the class divides into groups of 1-2 students (mostly pairs, maybe 1 student alone iirc) and takes a day to a few days to analyze one of the given poems. expectations/ how you should present/analyse it is made pretty clear and basically mimics the first few weeks of group analysis
midterm paper was in class (2 prompts to choose from, pick 1, everyone must do the last prompt, all about baudelaire/his writing; 2 about his work more conceptually (e.g., ideas he pioneered/ him in literary context), 1 about 2 of the poems we analyzed in class)

overall really easy. didn't really do any of the readings pre-class except for the presentation on my poem & prof is very forgiving time-wise. love her as a person too

reviews.content:
I'm pretty sure Queuniet didn't like me all too much. I forgot to turn in a vocab sheet quite in time, and she was pretty obviously miffed. 

That being said, I want to give her the highest possible recommendation! Sophie is a strong native speaker with an incredible vocabulary. She can call to memory random words, define them using only french, and still make it all interactive and fun. In a conversation class, you'd figure that there would be a lot of awkward silence, even from the professor, but it wasn't like that at all! She wasn't an overbearing, domineering professor that solely commanded the class. Nor was she a (pardon the French) laissez-faire professor, leaving it all to the students. Sophie was the excellent medium; she managed to steer conversations effortlessly from topic to topic, leaving all students satisfied. She brought in some french students to talk to, played "Taboo" with us, broadened our vocabulary immensely, and forced us to speak only in French. She was an excellently versatile professor, able to handle everything. 

That being said, she was by NO means an easy-A professor. If you struggle with vocab every so often like I do, she can be pretty brutal on quizzes. I haven't heard of any other Conv. Fr. teacher that gives quizzes yet. She also judges your presentations pretty harshly, but makes excellent criticism points. She wasn't an easy teacher, but if you really, really wanna improve your French, she's the professor to do it. 

The thing she did best was pronunciation - Sophie had a website that she would use to play little games to test our pronunciation. There were even some questions about it on our quizzes! My pronunciation was about a million times better at the end than it was at the beginning, and I'd considered myself fairly strong in that area. 

What a wonderful French teacher. To top it off, she brought us breakfast on the last day of class! Really cannot urge you enough: TAKE THIS DAMN CLASS.

Petits Interros - 15% (really challenging!)
